śīta-raśmi-kiraṇa-rajju-dolā-paribhraṣṭa-mūrchita iva apsaro-gaṇaḥ svaira-suptaḥ sundarī-janaḥ kā ca iyaṃ devi īva aravinda-hastā śārada-śaśa-aṅka-maṇḍala-amala-dukūla-uttara-cchadam adhiśete śayana-talam | na tāvad eṣā deva-yoṣā yato manda-mandam indu-kiraṇaiḥ samvāhyamānā kamalini īva saṅkucati | bhagna-vṛnta-cyuta-rasa-bindu-śabalitaṃ pāka-pāṇḍu-cūta-phalam iva udbhinna-sveda-rekham ālakṣyate gaṇḍa-sthalam | abhinava-yauvana-vidāha-nirbhara-ūṣmaṇi kuca-taṭe vaivarṇyam upaiti varṇakam | vāsasī ca paribhoga-anurūpaṃ dhūsarimāṇam ādarśayataḥ | tad eṣā mānuṣy- eva | diṣṭyā ca an-ucchiṣṭa-yauvanā yataḥ saukumāryam āgatāḥ samhatā iva avayavāḥ prasnigdhatamā api pāṇḍutā-anuviddha īva deha-cchaviḥ danta-pīḍā-an-abhijñatayā na ati-viśada-rāgo mukhe vidruma-dyutir adhara-maṇiḥ an-aty-āpūrṇam ārakta-mūlaṃ campaka-kuḍmala-dalam iva kaṭhoraṃ kapola-talam an-aṅga-bāṇa-pāta-mukta-āśaṅkaṃ ca viśrabdha-madhuraṃ supyate na ca etad-vakṣaḥ-sthalaṃ nir-daya-vimarda-vistārita-mukha-stana-yugalam asti ca an-ati krānta-śiṣṭa-maryāda-cetaso mama asyām āsaktiḥ | āsakty-anurūpaṃ punar āśliṣṭā yadi spaṣṭam ārta-raveṇa eva saha nidrāṃ mokṣyati | atha ahaṃ na śakṣyāmi ca an-upaśliṣya śayitum | ato yad bhāvi tad bhavatu | bhāgyam atra parīkṣiṣye | ' iti spṛṣṭa-a-spṛṣṭam eva kim apy āviddha-rāga-sādhvasaṃ lakṣya-suptaḥ sthito 'smi | sā api kim apy utkampinā roma-udbhedavatā vāma-pārśvena sukhāyamānena manda-manda-jṛmbhita-kārambha-manthara-aṅgī tvaṅgad-agra-pakṣmaṇoś cakṣuṣor alasa-tānta-tārakeṇa an-atipakva-nidrā-kaṣāyita-apāṅga-para-bhāgeṇa yugalenā iṣad unmilantī trāsa-vismaya-harṣa-rāga-śaṅkā-vilāsa-vibhrama-vyavahitāni vrīḍā-antarāṇi kāni kāny api kāmena adbhuta-anubhāvena avasthā-antarāṇi kāryamāṇā parijana-prabodhana-udyatā giraṃ kāma-āvega-para-vaśaṃ hṛdayam aṅgāni ca sādhvasa-āyāsa-sambadhyamāna-sveda-pulakāni kathaṃ katham api nigṛhya sa-spṛheṇa madhura-kūṇita-tri-bhāgeṇa manda-manda-pracāritena cakṣuṣā mad-aṅgāni nirvarṇya dūra-utsarpita-pūrva-kāyā api tasminn eva śayane sa-cakitam aśayiṣṭa | ajaniṣṭa me rāga-āviṣṭa-cetaso 'pi kim api nidrā | punar an-anukūla-sparśa-duḥkha-āyatta-gātraḥ prābudhye | prabuddhasya ca me sa aiva mahā-aṭavī tad eva taru-talaṃ sa eva patra-āstaro 'bhūt | vibhāvarī ca vyabhāsīt | abhūc ca me manasi - ' kim ayaṃ svapnaḥ kiṃ vipralambho vā kim iyam āsurī daivī vā kā api māyā | yad bhāvi tad bhavatu | na aham idaṃ tatvato na avabudhya mokṣyāmi bhūmi-śayyām | yāvad-āyur atratyāyai devatāyai pratiśayito bhavāmi ' iti niścita-matir atiṣṭham |

athāvirbhūya kā api ravikarābhitaptakuvalayadāmatāntāṅgayaṣṭiḥ kliṣṭanivasanottarīyā niralaktakarūkṣapāṭalena niḥśvāsoṣmajarjaritatviṣā dantacchadena vamantīva virahānalam anavaratasaliladhārāvisarjanād rudhirāvaśeṣam iva lohitataraṃ dvitayam akṣṇor udvahantī kulacāritrabandhanapāśavibhrameṇaikaveṇībhūtena keśapāśena nīlāmśukacīracūḍikāparivṛtā pativratāpatākeva sañcarantī kṣāmakṣāmā api devatānubhāvād anatikṣīṇavarṇāvakāśā sīmantinī praṇipatantaṃ māṃ praharṣotkampitena bhujalatādvayenotthāpya putravat pariṣvajya śirasy upāghrāya vātsalyam iva stanayugalena stanyacchalāt prakṣarantī śiśireṇa aśruṇā niruddhakaṇṭhī snehagadgadaṃ vyāhārṣīt - ' vatsa yadi vaḥ kathitavatī magadharājamahiṣī vasumatī mama haste bālam arthapālaṃ nidhāya kathāṃ ca kāñcid ātmabhartṛputrasakhījanānubaddhāṃ rājarājapravartitāṃ kṛtvā antardhānam agād ātmajā maṇibhadrasyeti sā aham asmi vo jananī | pitur vo dharmapālasūnoḥ sumitrānujasya kāmapālasya pādamūlān niṣkāraṇakopakaluṣitāśayā proṣya anuśayavidhurā svapne kena api rakṣorūpeṇopetya śaptā asmi - ' caṇḍikāyāṃ tvayi varṣamātraṃ vasāmi pravāsaduḥkhāya ' iti bruvataiva aham āviṣṭā prābudhye | gataṃ ca tad varṣaṃ varṣasahasradīrgham | atītāyāṃ tu yāminyāṃ devadevasya tryambakasya śrāvastyām utsavasamājam anubhūya bandhujanaṃ ca sthānasthānebhyaḥ samnipatitam abhisamīkṣya muktaśāpā patyuḥ pārśvam abhisarāmīti prasthitāyām eva mayi tvam atra abhyupetya ' prapanno asmi śaraṇam ihatyāṃ devatām ' iti prasuptoasi | evaṃ śāpaduḥkhāviṣṭayā tu mayā tadā na tatvataḥ paricchinno bhavān | api tu śaraṇāgatam aviralapramādāyām asyāṃ mahāṭavyām ayuktaṃ parityajya gantum iti mayā tvam api svapann eva asi nītaḥ | pratyāsanne ca tasmin devagṛhe punar acintayam - ' katham iha taruṇena anena saha samājaṃ gamiṣyāmi ' iti | atha rājñaḥ śrāvastīśvarasya yathārthanāmno dharmavardhanasya kanyāṃ navamālikāṃ gharmakālasubhage kanyāpuravimānaharmyatale viśālakomalaṃ śayyātalam adhiśayānāṃ yadṛcchayopalabhya ' diṣṭyeyaṃ suptā parijanaś ca gāḍhanidraḥ | śetām ayam atra muhūrtamātraṃ brāhmaṇakumāro yāvat kṛtakṛtyā nivarteya ' iti tvāṃ tatra śāyayitvā tam uddeśam agamam | dṛṣṭvā cotsavaśriyam nirviśya ca svajanadarśanasukham abhivādya ca tribhuvaneśvaram ātmālīkapratyākalanopārūḍhasādhvasaṃ ca namaskṛtya bhaktipraṇatahṛdayā bhagavatīm ambikāṃ tayā giriduhitrā devyā sasmitam ' ayi bhadre mā bhaiṣīḥ | bhavedānīṃ bhartṛpārśvagāminī | gatas te śāpaḥ ity anugṛhītā sadya eva pratyāpannamahimā pratinivṛtya dṛṣṭvaiva tvāṃ yathāvad abhyajānām  ' kathaṃ matsuta eva ayaṃ vatsasya arthapālasya prāṇabhūtaḥ sakhā pramatir iti | pāpayā mayā asminn ajñānād audāsīnyam ācaritam api ca ayam asyām āsaktabhāvaḥ | kanyā cainaṃ kāmayate yuvānam | ubhau cemau lakṣyasuptau trapayā sādhvasena vā anyoanyam ātmānaṃ na vivṛṇvāte | gantavyaṃ ca mayā | kāmāghrātayā apy anayā kanyayā rahasyarakṣaṇāya na samābhāṣitaḥ sakhījanaḥ parijano vā | nayāmi tāvat kumāram | punar apīmam arthaṃ labdhalakṣo yathopapannair upāyaiḥ sādhayiṣyati ' iti matprabhāvaprasvāpitaṃ bhavantam etad eva patraśayanam pratyanaiṣam | evam idaṃ vṛttam | eṣā ca ahaṃ pitus te pādamūlaṃ pratyupasarpeyam ' iti prāñjaliṃ māṃ bhūyo bhūyaḥ pariṣvajya śirasy upāghrāya kapolayoś cumbitvā snehavihvalā gatāsīt |
children.translated_text: Then a certain woman appeared—her slender body languid like a garland of blue lotuses scorched by the sun's rays, her garments and upper cloth worn and soiled, her lower lip pallid and rough without lac-dye, its luster shattered by the hot breath of her sighs, as though vomiting the fire of separation; bearing in both eyes a redness deeper than blood, as if from the unceasing discharge of streams of tears; her mass of hair, through the loosening of the binding cord of family propriety, become a single braid; wrapped in a crest-cloth of dark-blue bark-garments, she moved about like a banner of wifely devotion. Though exceedingly emaciated, by divine power her complexion and beauty were not entirely diminished. That noble woman, raising me as I prostrated before her with both vine-like arms trembling with sudden delight, embraced me like a son, smelled the top of my head, and, as though pouring out motherly love through both her breasts under the pretext of milk, her throat choked with cool tears, she spoke in a voice faltering with affection: 'My child, if the queen of the <s>Magadha</s> king, <s>Vasumatī</s>, has told you that she placed the boy <s>Arthapāla</s> in my hands, related a certain tale involving herself, her husband, son, and circle of friends, and set it in motion through the king of kings, and then vanished—she being the daughter of <s>Maṇibhadra</s>—then I am that very one; I am your mother. Having departed from the feet of your father <s>Kāmapāla</s>, son of <s>Dharmapāla</s> and younger brother of <s>Sumitrā</s>, my mind sullied by causeless anger, and being stricken with remorse, I was cursed in a dream by some being in the form of a <s>rākṣasa</s> who approached me and said: "O fierce woman, in you I shall dwell for one year, for the suffering of exile." Even as he was speaking, I was possessed, and I awoke. And that year passed, long as a thousand years. But on the night that has now passed, having experienced the festival-gathering of the God of Gods, the Three-Eyed <s>Tryambaka</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), at <s>Śrāvastī</s>, and having seen my kinsmen assembled from various places, I was freed from the curse. As I set forth intending to return to my husband's side, you arrived here and, saying "I take refuge in the local deity," fell asleep. But I, afflicted by the suffering of the curse, did not at that time properly recognize you. However, thinking it improper to abandon one who had sought refuge in this great forest teeming with constant dangers, I carried you—still sleeping—by my own power. And when we drew near to that temple, I thought again: "How can I go to the festival-gathering with this young man?" Then, by chance finding <s>Navamālikā</s>, the daughter of King <s>Dharmavardhana</s> of <s>Śrāvastī</s>—whose name befits him—sleeping upon a spacious, soft bed on the terrace of a pleasure-palace in the royal ladies' quarter, lovely in the summer season, [I thought]: "Fortunately she is asleep, and her attendants are in deep sleep. Let this <s>brāhmaṇa</s> youth lie here for just a moment while I fulfill my purpose and return." Having laid you down there, I went to that place. And having beheld the splendor of the festival, having enjoyed the happiness of seeing my own kinfolk, having paid reverence to the Lord of the Three Worlds, and having bowed with devotion in my heart to the Blessed Goddess <s>Ambikā</s> (Mother)—trembling with anxiety at the prospect of resuming my own illusory form—that daughter of the Mountain, the Goddess, with a smile said: "O good woman, do not be afraid! You shall now go to your husband's side. Your curse is ended." Thus blessed, my glory immediately restored, I returned and the moment I saw you, I recognized you properly: "How is this? This is none other than my own son—the dearest friend of my dear <s>Arthapāla</s>, named <s>Pramati</s>!" Wretched me, I had treated him with indifference out of ignorance! And moreover, he has become attached to this [maiden], and the maiden desires this young man. And both of them, caught asleep, from modesty or timidity do not reveal themselves to one another. And I must go. And she, this maiden, though her passion has been aroused, has not confided in her circle of friends or attendants, for the sake of guarding the secret. Let me take the prince away; eventually, having found the opportunity, he will accomplish this matter by whatever means present themselves.' Thus, by my power having put you to sleep, I brought you back to this very leaf-bed. Such is what happened. And now I shall go to approach the feet of your father.' So saying, she embraced me again and again as I stood with palms joined, smelled the top of my head, kissed both my cheeks, and departed, overcome with affection.

children.text: athā avirbhūya kā api ravi-kara-abhitapta-kuvalaya-dāma-tānta-aṅga-yaṣṭiḥ kliṣṭa-nivasana-uttarīyā nir-alaktaka-rūkṣa-pāṭalena niḥśvāsa-ūṣma-jarjarita-tviṣā danta-cchadena vamanti īva viraha-analam an-avarata-salila-dhārā-visarjanād rudhira-avaśeṣam iva lohitataraṃ dvitayam akṣṇor udvahantī kula-cāritra-bandhana-pāśa-vibhrameṇa eka-veṇībhūtena keśa-pāśena nīla-amśuka-cīra-cūḍikā-parivṛtā pati-vratā-patāka īva sañcarantī kṣāma-kṣāmā api devatā-anubhāvād an-atikṣīṇa-varṇa-avakāśā sīmantinī praṇipatantaṃ māṃ praharṣa-utkampitena bhuja-latā-dvayena utthāpya putra-vat pariṣvajya śirasy upāghrāya vātsalyam iva stana-yugalena stanya-cchalāt prakṣarantī śiśireṇa aśruṇā niruddha-kaṇṭhī sneha-gadgadaṃ vyāhārṣīt -- ' vatsa yadi vaḥ kathitavatī magadha-rāja-mahiṣī vasumatī mama haste bālam artha-pālaṃ nidhāya kathāṃ ca kāñ-cid ātma-bhartṛ-putra-sakhī-jana-anubaddhāṃ rāja-rāja-pravartitāṃ kṛtvā antar-dhānam agād ātmajā maṇi-bhadrasya iti sā aham asmi vo jananī | pitur vo dharma-pāla-sūnoḥ sumitrā-anujasya kāma-pālasya pāda-mūlān niṣ-kāraṇa-kopa-kaluṣita-āśayā proṣya anuśaya-vidhurā svapne kena api rakṣo-rūpeṇa upetya śaptā asmi -- ' caṇḍikāyāṃ tvayi varṣa-mātraṃ vasāmi pravāsa-duḥkhāya ' iti bruvata aiva aham āviṣṭā prābudhye | gataṃ ca tad varṣaṃ varṣa-sahasra-dīrgham | atītāyāṃ tu yāminyāṃ deva-devasya try-ambakasya śrāvastyām utsava-samājam anubhūya bandhu-janaṃ ca sthāna-sthānebhyaḥ samnipatitam abhisamīkṣya mukta-śāpā patyuḥ pārśvam abhisarāmi iti prasthitāyām eva mayi tvam atra abhyupetya ' prapanno asmi śaraṇam ihatyāṃ devatām ' iti prasuptoasi | evaṃ śāpa-duḥkha-āviṣṭayā tu mayā tadā na tatvataḥ paricchinno bhavān | api tu śaraṇa-āgatam a-virala-pramādāyām asyāṃ mahā-aṭavyām a-yuktaṃ parityajya gantum iti mayā tvam api svapann eva asi nītaḥ | pratyāsanne ca tasmin deva-gṛhe punar acintayam -- ' katham iha taruṇena anena saha samājaṃ gamiṣyāmi ' iti | atha rājñaḥ śrāvastī-īśvarasya yathā-artha-nāmno dharma-vardhanasya kanyāṃ nava-mālikāṃ gharma-kāla-subhage kanyā-pura-vimāna-harmya-tale viśāla-komalaṃ śayyā-talam adhiśayānāṃ yad-ṛcchaya ūpalabhya ' diṣṭya īyaṃ suptā parijanaś ca gāḍha-nidraḥ | śetām ayam atra muhūrta-mātraṃ brāhmaṇa-kumāro yāvat kṛta-kṛtyā nivarteya ' iti tvāṃ tatra śāyayitvā tam uddeśam agamam | dṛṣṭvā ca utsava-śriyam nirviśya ca sva-jana-darśana-sukham abhivādya ca tri-bhuvana-īśvaram ātma-alīka-pratyākalana-upārūḍha-sādhvasaṃ ca namaskṛtya bhakti-praṇata-hṛdayā bhagavatīm ambikāṃ tayā giri-duhitrā devyā sa-smitam ' ayi bhadre mā bhaiṣīḥ | bhava idānīṃ bhartṛ-pārśva-gāminī | gatas te śāpaḥ ity anugṛhītā sadya eva pratyāpanna-mahimā pratinivṛtya dṛṣṭva aiva tvāṃ yathāvad abhyajānām - ' kathaṃ mat-suta eva ayaṃ vatsasya artha-pālasya prāṇa-bhūtaḥ sakhā pramatir iti | pāpayā mayā asminn a-jñānād audāsīnyam ācaritam api ca ayam asyām āsakta-bhāvaḥ | kanyā ca enaṃ kāmayate yuvānam | ubhau ca imau lakṣya-suptau trapayā sādhvasena vā anyo-anyam ātmānaṃ na vivṛṇvāte | gantavyaṃ ca mayā | kāma-āghrātayā apy anayā kanyayā rahasya-rakṣaṇāya na samābhāṣitaḥ sakhī-janaḥ parijano vā | nayāmi tāvat kumāram | punar api imam arthaṃ labdha-lakṣo yatha ūpapannair upāyaiḥ sādhayiṣyati ' iti mat-prabhāva-prasvāpitaṃ bhavantam etad eva patra-śayanam pratyanaiṣam | evam idaṃ vṛttam | eṣā ca ahaṃ pitus te pāda-mūlaṃ pratyupasarpeyam ' iti prāñjaliṃ māṃ bhūyo bhūyaḥ pariṣvajya śirasy upāghrāya kapolayoś cumbitvā sneha-vihvalā gatā āsīt |

ahaṃ ca pañcabāṇavaśyaḥ śrāvastīm abhyavartiṣi | mārge ca mahati nigame naigamānāṃ tāmracūḍayuddhakolāhalo mahān āsīt | ahaṃ ca tatra samnihitaḥ kiñcid asmeṣi | samnidhiniṣaṇṇas tu me vṛddhaviṭaḥ ko 'pi brāhmaṇaḥ śanaiḥ smitahetum apṛcchat | abravaṃ ca  ' katham iva nārikelajāteḥ prācyavāṭakukkuṭasya pratīcyavāṭaḥ puruṣair asamīkṣya balākājātis tāmracūḍo balapramāṇādhikasyaiva prativisṛṣṭaḥ iti | so 'pi tajjñaḥ ' kim ajñair ebhir vyutpāditaiḥ | tūṣṇīm āssva ' ity upahastikāyās tāmbūlaṃ karpūrasahitam uddhṛtya mahyaṃ datvā citrāḥ kathāḥ kathayan kṣaṇam atiṣṭhat | prāyudhyata ca atisamrabdham anuprahārapravṛttasvapakṣamuktakaṇṭhīravaravaṃ vihaṅgamadvayam | jitaś ca asau pratīcyavāṭakukkuṭaḥ | so 'pi viṭabrāhmaṇaḥ svavāṭakukkuṭavijayahṛṣṭo mayi vayoviruddhaṃ sakhyam upetya tadahaḥ svagṛhae eva snānabhojanādi kārayitvottaredyuḥ śrāvastīṃ prati yāntaṃ mām anugamya ' smartavyo 'si saty arthe iti mitravad visṛjya pratyayāsīt |
children.translated_text: And I, under the sway of the five-arrowed one (<s>Pañcabāṇa</s> / <s>Kāma</s>), made my way toward <s>Śrāvastī</s>. On the road, in a great market-town, there was a tremendous uproar among the townspeople over a cockfight between red-crested roosters. I was present there and smiled a little. But an elderly libertine (<s>viṭa</s>), some <s>brāhmaṇa</s> who was seated near me, quietly asked the reason for my smile. I said: 'How is it that, for this rooster of the <s>nārikela</s> (coconut) breed from the eastern ward, a red-crested one of the <s>balākā</s> (crane) breed from the western ward has been released as opponent by people who have not assessed the strength — one that is clearly superior in fighting power?' He too, being a connoisseur, [said]: 'What use being instructed by these ignoramuses? Sit quietly.' Taking <s>tāmbūla</s> (betel) together with camphor from his pouch, he gave it to me and, telling fascinating stories, stayed for a while. And the two birds fought most furiously, the partisans of each releasing lion-like roars. And that rooster from the western ward was defeated. That libertine <s>brāhmaṇa</s>, delighted by the victory of his own ward's rooster, formed a friendship with me — incongruous given the difference in our ages — and on that very day, having arranged bathing, food, and the rest at his own house, on the following day accompanied me as I set out for <s>Śrāvastī</s>, and bidding me farewell as a friend with the words 'Remember me when there is true need,' he turned back.

children.text: ahaṃ ca pañca-bāṇa-vaśyaḥ śrāvastīm abhyavartiṣi | mārge ca mahati nigame naigamānāṃ tāmra-cūḍa-yuddha-kolāhalo mahān āsīt | ahaṃ ca tatra samnihitaḥ kiñ-cid asmeṣi | samnidhi-niṣaṇṇas tu me vṛddha-viṭaḥ ko 'pi brāhmaṇaḥ śanaiḥ smita-hetum apṛcchat | abravaṃ ca - ' katham iva nārikela-jāteḥ prācya-vāṭa-kukkuṭasya pratīcya-vāṭaḥ puruṣair a-samīkṣya balākā-jātis tāmra-cūḍo bala-pramāṇa-adhikasya eva prativisṛṣṭaḥ iti | so 'pi taj-jñaḥ ' kim a-jñair ebhir vyutpāditaiḥ | tūṣṇīm āssva ' ity upahastikāyās tāmbūlaṃ karpūra-sahitam uddhṛtya mahyaṃ datvā citrāḥ kathāḥ kathayan kṣaṇam atiṣṭhat | prāyudhyata ca ati-samrabdham anuprahāra-pravṛtta-sva-pakṣa-mukta-kaṇṭhīrava-ravaṃ vihaṅgama-dvayam | jitaś ca asau pratīcya-vāṭa-kukkuṭaḥ | so 'pi viṭa-brāhmaṇaḥ sva-vāṭa-kukkuṭa-vijaya-hṛṣṭo mayi vayo-viruddhaṃ sakhyam upetya tad-ahaḥ sva-gṛhae eva snāna-bhojana-ādi kārayitva ūttare-dyuḥ śrāvastīṃ prati yāntaṃ mām anugamya ' smartavyo 'si saty arthe iti mitravad visṛjya pratyayāsīt |

ahaṃ ca gatvā śrāvastīm adhvaśrānto bāhyodyāne latāmaṇḍape śayito 'smi | hamsakaravaprabodhitaś cotthāya kām api kvaṇitanūpuramukharābhyāṃ caraṇābhyāṃ madantikam upasarantīṃ yuvatīm adrākṣam | sā tv āgatya svahastavartini citrapaṭe likhitaṃ matsadṛśaṃ kim api puṃrūpaṃ māṃ ca paryāyeṇa nirvarṇayantī savismayaṃ savitarkaṃ saharṣaṃ ca kṣaṇam avātiṣṭhata | mayā api tatra citrapaṭe matsādṛśyaṃ paśyatā taddṛṣṭiceṣṭitam anākasmikaṃ manyamānena ' nanu sarvasādhāraṇo 'yaṃ ramaṇīyaḥ puṇyārāmabhūmibhāgaḥ | kim iti cirasthitikleśoanubhūyate | nanūpaveṣṭavyam ' ity abhihitā sā sasmitam ' anugṛhītā asmi ' iti nyaṣīdat | saṅkathā ca deśavārtānubaddhā kācanāvayor abhūt | kathāsamśritā ca sā ' deśātithir asi | dṛśyante ca te 'dhvaśrāntānīva gātrāṇi | yadi na doṣo madgṛhe 'dya viśramitum anugrahaḥ kriyatām ' ity aśamsat | ahaṃ ca ' ayi mugdhe naiṣa doṣo guṇa eva ' iti tadanumārgagāmī tadgṛhagato rājārheṇa snānabhojanādinopacaritaḥ sukhaṃ niṣaṇṇo rahasi paryapṛcchye - ' mahābhāga digantarāṇi bhramatā kaccid asti kiñcid adbhutaṃ bhavatopalabdham ' iti | mama abhavan manasi - ' mahad idam āśāspadam | eṣā khalu nikhilaparijanasambādhasamlakṣitāyāḥ sakhī rājadārikāyāḥ citrapaṭe ca asminn api tadupariviracitasitavitānaṃ harmyatalam tadgataṃ ca prakāmavistīrṇaṃ śaradabhrapaṭalapāṇḍuraṃ śayanam tadadhiśāyinī ca nidrālīḍhalocanā mamaiveyaṃ pratikṛtiḥ | ato nūnam anaṅgena sā api rājakanyā tāvatīṃ bhūmim āropitā yasyām asahyamadanajvaravyathitonmāditā satī sakhīnirbandhapṛṣṭavikriyānimittā cāturyeṇaitadrūpanirmāṇenaiva samartham uttaraṃ dattavatī | rūpasamvādāc ca samśayānayā anayā pṛṣṭo bhindyām asyāḥ samśayaṃ yathānubhavakathanena ' iti jātaniścayo 'bravam - ' bhadre dehi citrapaṭam ' iti | sā tv arpitavatī maddhaste | punas tam ādāya tām api vyājasuptām ullasanmadanarāgavihvalāṃ vallabhām ekatraiva abhilikhya ' kācid evaṃbhūtā yuvatir īdṛśasya pumsaḥ pārśvaśāyiny araṇyānīprasuptena mayopalabdhā | kilaiṣa svapnaḥ ' ity ālapaṃ ca | hṛṣṭayā tu tayā vistarataḥ pṛṣṭaḥ sarvam eva vṛttāntam akathayam | asau ca sakhyā mannimittāny avasthāntarāṇy avarṇayat | tad ākarṇya ca ' yadi tava sakhyā madanugrahonmukhaṃ mānasam gamaya kānicid ahāni | kam api kanyāpure nirāśaṅkanivāsakaraṇam upāyam āracayyāgamiṣyāmi ' iti kathañcid enām abhyupagamayya gatvā tad eva kharvaṭaṃ vṛddhaviṭena samagaṃsi |
children.translated_text: And having gone to <s>Śrāvastī</s>, exhausted from the journey, I lay down in a creeper-bower in an outer garden. Awakened by the sound of a goose, I rose and beheld a certain young woman approaching me, her feet made resonant by jingling anklets. She, having come close, examined alternately a portrait of some male figure resembling me, painted on a canvas held in her own hand, and me — and remained for a moment in a state of wonder, speculation, and joy. I too, seeing the resemblance to me in that canvas portrait, considering her gaze and gestures to be no coincidence, said: 'Is this not a pleasant and holy garden-ground, open to all? Why endure the discomfort of standing so long? Pray, do be seated.' She, with a smile, said 'I am obliged' and sat down. And some conversation of ours arose, following the topic of local news. And she, weaving [her intention] into the conversation, said: 'You are a visitor from another region. And your limbs appear weary from travel. If there is no impropriety, please do me the favor of resting today at my house.' And I said: 'O naive one, this is no impropriety — it is a virtue indeed,' and following her path, I went to her house. Having been attended with bathing, food, and the rest befitting a king, I sat comfortably and was asked in private: 'O great-fortuned one, wandering in distant lands, have you by chance encountered anything wonderful?' In my mind arose [the thought]: 'This is a great opportunity! She is clearly the friend of a princess, as perceived by the whole retinue around her. And in this canvas, on the terrace-floor of a palace depicted above her [the princess], with a white canopy spread over it, there is a spacious bed, pale as a sheet of autumn clouds, and reclining upon it, with eyes half-closed in drowsiness — this is a portrait of none other than myself! Therefore, surely by the power of <s>Anaṅga</s> (the god of love), that princess too has been brought to such a pitch that, maddened and tormented by unbearable love-fever, when pressed by her friend about the cause of her changed state, she cleverly gave a sufficient answer by means of creating this very portrait. And this woman, recognizing the resemblance of form but still uncertain, has questioned me. I should dispel her doubt by narrating my own experience.' Having thus resolved, I said: 'Good woman, give me the canvas.' And she placed it in my hand. Taking it, I then sketched on it that same beloved — pretending to be asleep, yet flushed with the agitation of surging passion — lying beside just such a man, and said: 'Some such young woman was found sleeping beside such a man in a forest when I was asleep. Such was my dream, it seems.' And she, delighted, questioned me at length, and I told the entire story. And she described the changes of state in her friend on my account. Hearing that, I said: 'If your friend's heart is inclined to favor me, spend a few days. I shall devise some stratagem for dwelling without suspicion in the maiden's quarter, and I will come.' Somehow persuading her thus, I went to that very market-town and met the elderly libertine (<s>viṭa</s>).

a-sahya-madana-jvara-vyathita-unmāditā satī sakhī-nirbandha-pṛṣṭa-vikriyā-nimittā cāturyeṇa etad-rūpa-nirmāṇena eva samartham uttaraṃ dattavatī | rūpa-samvādāc ca samśayānayā anayā pṛṣṭo bhindyām vallabhām ekatra eva abhilikhya ' kā-cid evaṃ-bhūtā yuvatir īdṛśasya pumsaḥ pārśva-śāyiny- araṇyānī-prasuptena maya ūpalabdhā | kila eṣa svapnaḥ ' ity ālapaṃ ca | hṛṣṭayā tu tayā vistarataḥ pṛṣṭaḥ nir-āśaṅka-nivāsa-karaṇam upāyam āracayyā agamiṣyāmi ' iti kathañ-cid enām abhyupagamayya gatvā tad eva kharvaṭaṃ vṛddha-viṭena samagaṃsi |

so 'pi sasambhramaṃ viśramayya tathaiva snānabhojanādi kārayitvā rahasy apṛcchat - ' ārya kasya hetor acireṇaiva pratyāgato 'si | ' pratyavādiṣam enam  ' sthānae eva aham āryeṇa asmi pṛṣṭaḥ | śrūyatām | asti hi śrāvastī nāma nagarī | tasyāḥ patir apara iva dharmaputro dharmavardhano nāma rājā | tasya duhitā pratyādeśa iva śriyaḥ prāṇā iva kusumadhanvanaḥ saukumāryaviḍambitanavamālikā vanamālikā nāma kanyā | sā mayā samāpattidṛṣṭā kāmanārācapaṅktim iva kaṭākṣamālāṃ mama marmaṇi vyakirat | tacchalyoddharaṇakṣamaś ca dhanvantarisadṛśas tvad ṛte netaro 'sti vaidya iti pratyāgato 'smi | tat prasīda kañcid upāyam ācaritum | ayam ahaṃ parivartitastrīveṣas te kanyā nāma bhaveyam | anugataś ca mayā tvam upagamya dharmāsanagataṃ dharmavardhanaṃ vakṣyasi - ' mameyam ekaiva duhitā | jātamātrāyāṃ tv asyāṃ janany asyāḥ saṃsthitā | mātā ca pitā ca bhūtvā aham eva vyavardhayam | etadartham eva vidyāmayaṃ śulkam arjituṃ gato abhūd avantinagarīm ujjayinīm asmadvaivāhyakulajaḥ ko 'pi vipradārakaḥ | tasmai ceyam anumatā dātum itarasmai na yogyā | taruṇī bhūtā ceyam | sa ca vilambitaḥ | tena tam ānīya pāṇim asyā grāhayitvā tasmin nyastabhāraḥ samnyasiṣye | durabhirakṣatayā tu duhitrṇāṃ muktaśaiśavānāṃ viśeṣataś ca amātṛkāṇām iha devaṃ mātṛpitṛsthānīyaṃ prajānām āpannaśaraṇam āgato 'smi | yadi vṛddhaṃ brāhmaṇam adhītinam agatim atithiṃ ca mām anugrāhyapakṣe gaṇayaty ādirājacaritadhuryo devaḥ saiṣā bhavadbhujacchāyām akhaṇḍitacāritrā tāvad adhyāstāṃ yāvad asyāḥ pāṇigrāhakam ānayeyam ' iti | sa evam ukto niyatam abhimanāyamānaḥ svaduhitṛsamnidhau māṃ vāsayiṣyati | gatas tu bhavān āgāmini māsi phālgune phalgunīṣūttarāsu bhāvini rājāntaḥpurajanasya tīrthayātrotsave tīrthasnānāt prācyāṃ diśi gorutāntaram atikramya vānīravalayamadhyavartini kārttikeyagṛhe karatalagatena śuklāmbarayugalena sthāsyasi | sa khalv aham anabhiśaṅka evaitāvantaṃ kālaṃ saha abhivihṛtya rājakanyayā bhūyas tasminn utsave gaṅgāmbhasi viharan vihāravyākule kanyakāsamāje magnopasṛtas tvadabhyāsae evonmaṅkṣyāmi | punas tvadupahṛte vāsasī paridhāya apanītadārikāveṣo jāmātā nāma bhūtvā tvām eva anugaccheyam | nṛpātmajā tu mām itastato 'nviṣya anāsādayantī ' tayā vinā na bhokṣye ' iti rudaty eva avarodhane sthāsyati | tanmūle ca mahati kolāhale krandatsu parijaneṣu rudatsu sakhījaneṣu śocatsu paurajaneṣu kiṅkartavyatāmūḍhe sāmātye pārthive tvam āsthānīm etya māṃ sthāpayitvā vakṣyasi  ' deva sa eṣa me jāmātā tava arhati śrībhujārādhanam | adhītī caturṣv āmnāyeṣu gṛhītī ṣaṭsv aṅgeṣu ānvīkṣikīvicakṣaṇaḥ catuḥṣaṣṭikalāgamaprayogacaturaḥ viśeṣeṇa gajarathaturaṅgatantravit iṣvasanāstrakarmaṇi gadāyuddhe ca nirupamaḥ purāṇetihāsakuśalaḥ kartā kāvyanāṭakākhyāyikānām vettā sopaniṣado 'rthaśāstrasya nirmatsaro guṇeṣu viśrambhī suhṛtsu śakyaḥ samvibhāgaśīlaḥ śrutadharo gatasmayaś ca | na asya doṣam aṇīyāṃsam apy upalabhe | na ca guṇeṣv avidyamānam | tan mādṛśasya brāhmaṇamātrasya na labhya eṣa sambandhī | duhitaram asmai samarpya vārddhakocitam antyam āśramaṃ saṅkrameyam yadi devaḥ sādhu manyate ' iti | sa idam ākarṇya vaivarṇyākrāntavaktraḥ param upeto vailakṣyam ārapsyate 'nunetum anityatādisaṅkīrtanena atrabhavantaṃ mantribhiḥ saha | tvaṃ tu teṣām adattaśrotro muktakaṇṭhaṃ ruditvā cirasya bāṣpakuṇṭhakaṇṭhaḥ kāṣṭhāny āhṛtya agniṃ sandhukṣya rājamandiradvāre citādhirohaṇāyopakramiṣyase | sa tāvad eva tvatpādayor nipatya sāmātyo narapatir anūnair arthais tvām upacchandya duhitaraṃ mahyaṃ datvā madyogyatāsamārādhitaḥ samastam eva rājyabhāraṃ mayi samarpayiṣyati | so 'yam abhyupāyo 'nuṣṭheyaḥ yadi tubhyaṃ rocate ' iti | so 'pi paṭuviṭānām agraṇīr asakṛdabhyastakapaṭaprapañcaḥ pāñcālaśarmā yathoktam abhyadhikaṃ ca nipuṇam upakrāntavān | āsīc ca mama samīhitānām ahīnakālasiddhiḥ | anvabhavaṃ ca madhukara iva navamālikām ārdrasumanasam | asya rājñaḥ simhavarmaṇaḥ sāhāyyadānaṃ suhṛtsaṅketabhūmigamanam ity ubhayam apekṣya sarvabalasandohena campām imām upagato daivād devadarśanasukham anubhavāmi ' iti | śrutvaitatpramaticaritaṃ smitamukulitamukhanalinaḥ ' vilāsaprāyam ūrjitam mṛduprāyaṃ ceṣṭitam iṣṭa eṣa mārgaḥ prajñāvatām | athedānīm atra bhavān praviśatu iti mitraguptam aikṣata kṣitīśaputraḥ |
children.translated_text: He too, anxiously making me rest, and having me bathe and eat as before, asked me in private: 'Sir, why have you returned so quickly?' I replied to him: 'You have asked me the right question, sir. Listen! There is a city called <s>Śrāvastī</s>. Its lord is a king named <s>Dharmavardhana</s>, like another son of <s>Dharma</s> (Yudhiṣṭhira). His daughter — as if a rebuke to <s>Śrī's</s> beauty, as if the very life-breath of the Flower-Armed One (<s>Kāma</s>) — is a maiden named <s>Vanamālikā</s>, whose delicacy mocks a freshly blooming jasmine garland. I beheld her in a visionary trance, and she scattered across my vital parts a garland of sidelong glances like a volley of Desire's arrows. No physician other than you, who are like <s>Dhanvantari</s> himself, is capable of extracting that dart. That is why I have returned. So be gracious and devise some stratagem. I myself, having adopted feminine attire, shall become your so-called daughter. Accompanied by me, you shall approach <s>Dharmavardhana</s> seated upon his throne of justice and say: "This is my only daughter. Her mother died at the very moment of her birth. Being both mother and father, I alone raised her. For her sake, some brahmin youth of our marriage-alliance lineage went to the city of <s>Avanti</s>, <s>Ujjayinī</s>, to earn a bride-price through learning. To him she has been promised; she is not suitable for another. She has now become a young woman, yet he has delayed. Therefore, bringing him here and having him take her hand in marriage, I shall deposit my burden and renounce the world. But since unmarried daughters past childhood — especially those without a mother — are difficult to protect, I have come to the king, who stands in the place of mother and father to his subjects, the refuge of the distressed, and who follows the conduct of primeval kings. If His Majesty counts me — an aged, learned, shelterless, guest brahmin — among those worthy of his favor, then let this girl dwell under the protection of Your Majesty's arm, her virtue unimpaired, until I bring her bridegroom." Thus addressed, he will certainly, out of regard for his honor, lodge me near his own daughter. You, having gone away, shall return in the coming month of <s>Phālguna</s>, on the day of the <s>Uttara-Phalgunī</s> constellation, during the pilgrimage festival of the royal household. Having crossed a distance of one <s>goruta</s> (about two miles) east of the sacred bathing place, you shall stand in the temple of <s>Kārttikeya</s> situated within a circle of cane-thickets, holding a pair of white garments in your hands. I, having sported without suspicion for that long with the princess, shall, during that festival, while frolicking in the waters of the <s>Gaṅgā</s>, amidst the confusion of play and the commotion of the maidens' assembly, pretend to have drowned and shall emerge right near you. Then, putting on the garments you have brought and discarding the maiden's disguise, I shall become the so-called son-in-law and follow you. The princess, searching for me here and there but not finding me, will stand weeping in her chamber, crying: 'Without her I will not eat!' On that account, with great commotion — the attendants wailing, the friends lamenting, the townsfolk grieving, the king and his ministers bewildered with helplessness — you shall come to the royal court, present me, and say: 'Your Majesty, this is my son-in-law. He is worthy of the worship of Your Majesty's arm. He has studied the four <s>Vedas</s>, mastered the six <s>Vedāṅgas</s> (auxiliary sciences), is expert in logic (<s>ānvīkṣikī</s>), skilled in the theory and practice of the sixty-four arts, especially knowledgeable in the science of elephants, chariots, and horses, unrivaled in archery, missile-weapons, and mace-combat, versed in <s>Purāṇas</s> and <s>Itihāsas</s>, a composer of <s>kāvya</s>, <s>nāṭaka</s>, and <s>ākhyāyikā</s> (romances), a knower of the <s>Arthaśāstra</s> together with the <s>Upaniṣads</s>, free from envy, trusting toward friends, of generous disposition, retentive of learning, and without vanity. I find not even the slightest fault in him, nor any quality lacking. Such an alliance is not easily obtained by a mere brahmin like me. Having given my daughter to him, I would enter the final stage of life befitting old age, if His Majesty deems it proper.' He, hearing this, his face overcome with pallor and seized with the utmost embarrassment, will begin trying to dissuade the gentleman by extolling impermanence and the like, together with his ministers. But you, paying no heed to them, having wept aloud with abandon, shall after a while, with throat choked by tears, gather firewood, kindle a fire, and make preparations to mount the funeral pyre at the palace gate. At that very moment, the king together with his ministers, falling at your feet and appeasing you with lavish offerings, having given me his daughter and satisfied himself of my worthiness, will entrust the entire burden of the kingdom to me. This is the plan to be carried out, if it pleases you.' And he too — <s>Pāñcālaśarman</s>, the foremost among clever rogues, well-practiced in the art of deceit and pretense — carried out the plan as described, and even more skillfully. And my desires were accomplished at the proper time, without deficiency. And I enjoyed that tender-hearted one, soft as a fresh jasmine bloom, like a bee enjoying a new garland. With the dual purpose of rendering aid to this King <s>Siṃhavarman</s> and going to the meeting-place appointed by friends, I came to this <s>Campā</s> with my entire assembled forces, and by fortune I experience the happiness of beholding the Lord.' Having heard this tale of <s>Pramati</s>, the prince, his lotus-face gently blossoming with a smile, said: 'A conduct that is mainly graceful, vigorous yet mainly gentle — this is the cherished path of the wise. Now then, let this gentleman enter,' and he looked toward <s>Mitragupta</s>.

children.translated_text: He too began to tell: 'My lord, I too, seeking [you as] the common concern of all friends, came to the <s>Suhma</s> country and was watching a great festival-gathering in the public garden outside the city called <s>Dāmalipta</s>. There, in a certain bower of <s>atimukta</s> (jasmine) creepers, I saw a certain young man entertaining himself with the playing of a <s>vīṇā</s>, appearing anxious. I asked him: "Good sir, what is this festival called? For what purpose has it been arranged? And for what reason do you stand here in solitude, apparently anxious, with only a lute for companion, taking no part in the festival?" He replied: "My friend, the lord of the <s>Suhmas</s>, named <s>Tuṅgadhanvan</s>, being childless, prayed at this very shrine to the goddess <s>Vindhyavāsinī</s>, whose rage has been forgotten, for a pair of offspring. And she, so it is said, instructed him in a dream while he lay sleeping: 'One son will be born to you, and one daughter as well. He shall follow the husband she chooses. And she, from the seventh year until her marriage, on each monthly <s>Kṛttikā</s> [day], shall propitiate me with ball-dancing for the attainment of a worthy husband. And she shall be given to whomever she desires. And that festival shall be called the Ball Festival (<s>Kandukotsava</s>).' Then, in a short time, the king's beloved chief queen, named <s>Medinī</s>, gave birth to a son. And one daughter was also born. Today, that princess, named <s>Kandukāvatī</s>, will come to propitiate the goddess <s>Somāpīḍā</s> with ball-play. Now, her friend <s>Candrasenā</s>, a foster-sister, was my beloved. And in recent days she has been forcibly pursued by the prince <s>Bhīmadhanvan</s>. Therefore I am anxious, my mind tormented by the dart-wound of <s>Manmatha's</s> (Love's) arrow, somewhat soothing myself with the slow sound of the <s>vīṇā</s>, and sitting here in seclusion." At that very moment, the tinkling of jeweled anklets was heard. And a certain woman arrived. The moment he saw her, his eyes blooming wide, he rose and embraced her tightly; and she, clasping his neck, sat down there with him. And he confided: 'This is she, the equal of my life, whose separation burns me like fire. And the prince who robs me of my life has rendered me as cold as if by death itself. But I cannot commit a crime against a prince. Therefore, having had her look upon me one last time, I shall abandon these lives that are beyond remedy.' But she, tears on her face, responded: 'Do not, my lord, resolve on recklessness on my account. You, born from the excellent caravan-leader <s>Arthadāsa</s>, were given the name <s>Kośadāsa</s> (Treasury-Slave) by your elders, and then, because of your excessive attachment to me, have been publicly proclaimed <s>Veśadāsa</s> (Courtesan's Slave) by your enemies. If you were to die and I were to live, the world would harshly judge that I am a cruel courtesan. Therefore, this very day, take me to whatever land you desire.' But he addressed me: 'Good sir, of all the kingdoms you have seen, which is most prosperous, rich in harvests, and inhabited mostly by good people?' I answered him with a slight smile: 'Good sir, vast is this [world] girded by oceans. There is no end to the delightful provinces in various places. But if I cannot devise some plan that enables the two of you to live happily right here, then I myself would be a false guide.' Just then, the tinkling of jeweled anklets arose. And she, now in haste, said: 'The young mistress, Princess <s>Kandukāvatī</s>, has arrived to propitiate the goddess <s>Vindhyavāsinī</s> with ball-play. And viewing is unrestricted at this Ball Festival. May your eyes be rewarded! Come and watch. I shall be at her side.' And she departed. And we both followed her. Upon a great stage of jeweled platforms, I first beheld that red-lipped maiden. And she immediately took up residence in my heart. Neither I nor anyone else had seen [her like] in the interval. Filled with wonder, I thought: 'Is this <s>Lakṣmī</s> (the Goddess of Fortune)? No, no! For she, they say, holds a lotus placed in her hand, whereas this one's very hand is a lotus. And that one has been enjoyed by an ancient man, by former kings; but this one's youth is unblemished and fresh.' Even as I was thinking thus, she—all her limbs faultless—touching the ground with the tips of her spread finger-shoots of interlaced hands, her dark curling locks swaying, bowed gracefully to the Goddess, and then took hold of the ball—red-eyed with passion, like <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of Love) himself—and then released it to the ground with playful ease; and gently striking the slowly rising [ball] with her palm-shoot of slightly curled thumb and extended soft fingers, tossing it up with the back of her hand, catching the falling ball—marked with her flirtatious glance like a cluster [of flowers] strung by a garland of bees—right in mid-air, she released it again; striking softly, softly, with pauses in the middle and at rapid tempo, she displayed in that instant a powdered-step [dance]; and having calmed [the ball], she set it into motion again with merciless strikes; and in reverse, she stilled it; and catching the ball coming straight, she struck it alternately with left and right hands, making it soar like a bird; and striking the far-flying, falling [ball], she improvised a musical pattern; and sending it in every direction, she called it back. Thus sporting with a sweetness of manifold technique, the princess played most wondrously while receiving, moment by moment, the high and low words of praise from the audience seated in the arena, whose hearts were captivated; and leaning on the shoulder of <s>Kośadāsa</s>—who had at that instant assumed a bold intimacy—she faced toward me, whose cheeks were bristling [with excitement] and whose eyes were wide open; and just then, her sidelong glance first descended, shot by <s>Kāma</s> (Love), and along its path her playfully arched brow-creeper quivered; with the clusters of rays from her lips, set dancing by the force of the wind of her sighs—like playful palm-shoots—she seemed to strike the bees hovering eagerly to seize the fragrance of her face-lotus; in the circular whirlings of the ball, moving it so swiftly that she seemed to enter—out of modesty at my gaze—into a cage of flowers; when the ball flew in five directions at five points, she seemed to be warding off, as if in fright, five arrows of the Five-Arrowed One (<s>Kāma</s>) falling all at once; in zigzag movements, she displayed the vibrations of dense passion, mimicking a streak of lightning; her footwork synchronized with the rhythm given by the tinkling of the gems in her ornaments; her <s>bimba</s>-fruit lip suffused with the light of a smile under some pretext; her topknot loosened and re-gathered; her jeweled girdle-strings clashing and jingling; her garment—brilliant and fluttering—loosened and hanging from her broadly upraised hip as she bent and rose; the graceful ball struck by vine-like arms curling, extending, and waving; her arm-noose drawn back; her playful dangling curls clinging as she turned her waist; replacing the golden leaf earring that had slipped off—so swift in that replacement that it did not interrupt her natural play; the ball, thrown repeatedly by hands and feet, spinning inside and outside; her middle body-stalk disappearing in the unbroken sequence of bending and rising; her pearl necklace reversing position with each fall and rise; her cheek-painting smudged by the perspiration that had sprouted, the drying [of which was] entrusted to the leaf-fans at her ears; one palm-shoot engaged in controlling the garment slipping from the slope of her breasts—sitting and rising, closing and opening her eyes, standing and moving, the princess played most extraordinarily. Striking [the ball] both on ground and in air, she demonstrated various play-interludes, appearing to be many with just a single ball, though she was but one. And having sported with her dear friends <s>Candrasenā</s> and the others, and at the end of play having saluted the Goddess, directing toward me—with a mind as though filled with passion—a sidelong glance like a <s>kuvalaya</s> (blue lotus) arrow from the bow of the Flower-Arrowed One (<s>Kāma</s>), repeatedly turning the moon-disc of her face under some pretext as if to look whether her own heart, sent to my presence, had returned or not, she went with her companions to the royal maiden's quarters.

āgacchataṃ draṣṭum | aham asyāḥ sakāśa-vartinī bhaveyam ' ity ayāsīt | tām anvayāva cā avām | mahati ratna-raṅga-pīṭhe sthitāṃ prathamaṃ tāmra-oṣṭhīm apaśyam | atiṣṭhac ca sā sadya eva mama hṛdaye | pāṇi-pallavena samāhatya hasta-pṛṣṭhena ca unnīya caṭula-dṛṣṭi-lāñchitaṃ stabakam iva bhramara-mālā-anuviddham avapatantam ākāśae eva agrahīt | amuñcac ca | madhya-vilambita-laye druta-laye mṛdu-mṛdu ahaṃ ca anaṅgavihvalaḥ svaveśma gatvā kośadāsena yatnavad atyudāraṃ snānabhojanādikam anubhāvito 'smi | sāyaṃ copasṛtya candrasenā rahasi māṃ praṇipatya patyur amsam amsena praṇayapeśalam āghaṭṭayanty upādiśat | ācaṣṭa ca hṛṣṭaḥ kośadāsaḥ - ' bhūyāsam evam yāvadāyur āyatākṣi tvatprasādasya pātram iti | mayā tu sasmitam abhihitam - ' sakhe kim etad āśāsyam | asti kiñ=cid añjanam | anayā tadaktanetrayā rājasūnur upasthito vānarīm ivaināṃ drakṣyati viraktaś caināṃ punas tyakṣyati ' iti | tayā tu smerayā asmi kathitaḥ - ' so 'yam āryeṇājñākaro jano 'tyartham anugṛhītaḥ yad asminn eva janmani mānuṣaṃ vapur apanīya vānarīkariṣyate | tad āstām idam | anyathā api siddhaṃ naḥ samīhitam | adya khalu kandukotsave bhavantam avahasitamanobhavākāram abhilaṣantī roṣād iva śambaradviṣā atimātram āyāsyate rājaputrī | so 'yam artho viditabhāvayā mayā svamātre tayā ca tanmātre mahiṣyā ca manujendrāya nivedayiṣyate | viditārthas tu pārthivas tvayā duhituḥ pāṇiṃ grāhayiṣyati | tataś ca tvadanujīvinā rājaputreṇa bhavitavyam | eṣa hi devatāsamādiṣṭo vidhiḥ | tvadāyatte ca rājye na alam eva tvām atikramya mām avaroddhum bhīmadhanvā | tat sahatām ayaṃ tricaturāṇi dināni | ' iti mām āmantrya priyaṃ copagūhya pratyayāsīt | mama kośadāsasya ca taduktānusāreṇa bahu vikalpayatoḥ kathañ=cid akṣīyata kṣapā | kṣapānte ca kṛtayathocitaniyamas tam eva priyādarśanasubhagam udyānoddeśam upagato 'smi | tatraiva copasṛtya rājaputro nirabhimānam anukūlābhiḥ kathābhir mām anuvartamāno muhūrtam āsta | nītvā copakāryām ātmasamena snānabhojanaśayanādivyatikareṇopācarat | talpagataṃ ca svapnena anubhūyamānapriyādarśanāliṅganasukham āyasena nigaḍena atibalavadbahupuruṣaiḥ pīvarabhujadaṇḍoparuddham abandhayan mām | pratibuddhaṃ ca sahasā samabhyadhāt - ' ayi durmate śrutam ālapitaṃ hatāyāś candrasenāyā jālarandhraniḥsṛtaṃ tadekāvabodhaprayuktayā anayā kubjayā | tvaṃ kila abhilaṣito varākyā kandukavatyā tava kila anujīvinā mayā stheyam tvadvacaḥ kila anatikramatā mayā candrasenā kośadāsāya dāsyate ity uktvā pārśvacaraṃ puruṣam ekam ālokya akathayat - ' prakṣipainaṃ sāgare ' iti | sa tu labdharājya iva atihṛṣṭaḥ ' deva yad ājñāpayasi ' iti yathādiṣṭam akarot | ahaṃ tu nirālambano bhujābhyām itastataḥ spandamānaḥ kim=api kāṣṭhaṃ daivadattam urasopaśliṣya tāvad aploṣi yāvad apāsarad vāsaraḥ śarvarī ca sarvā | pratyuṣasy adṛśyata kim=api vahitram | amutrāsan yavanāḥ | te mām uddhṛtya rāmeṣunāmne nāvikanāyakāya kathitavantaḥ - ' ko 'py ayam āyasanigaḍabaddha eva jale labdhaḥ puruṣaḥ | so 'yam api siñcet sahasraṃ drākṣāṇāṃ kṣaṇenaikena iti | asminn eva kṣaṇe naikanaukāparivṛtaḥ ko 'pi madgur abhyadhāvat | abibhayur yavanāḥ | tāvad atijavā naukāḥ śvāna iva varāham asmatpotaṃ paryarutsata | prāvartata ca samprahāraḥ | parājāyiṣata yavanāḥ | tān aham agatīn avasīdataḥ samāśvāsya alapiṣam - ' apanayata me nigaḍabandhanam | ayam aham avasādayāmi vaḥ sapatnān ' iti | amī tathā akurvan | sarvāmś ca tān pratibhaṭān bhallavarṣiṇā bhīmaṭaṅkṛtena śārṅgeṇa lavalavīkṛtāṅgān akārṣam | avaplutya hatavidhvastayodham asmatpotasamsaktapotam amutra nāvikanāyakam anabhisaram abhipatya jīvagrāham agrahīṣam | asau cāsīt sa eva bhīmadhanvā | taṃ ca aham avabudhya jātavrīḍam abravam - ' tāta kiṃ dṛṣṭāni kṛtāntavilasitāni ' iti | te tu sāmyātrikā madīyenaiva śṛṅkhalena tam atigāḍhaṃ baddhvā harṣakilakilāravam akurvan māṃ ca apy apūjayan | durvārā tu sā naur ananukālavātanunnā dūram abhipatya kam api dvīpaṃ nibiḍam āśliṣṭavatī | tatra ca svādu pānīyam edhāmsi kandamūlaphalāni ca sañjighṛkṣavo gāḍhapātitaśilāvalayam avātarāma | tatra cāsīn mahāśailaḥ | so 'ham - ' aho ramaṇīyo 'yaṃ parvatanitambabhāgaḥ kāntatareyaṃ gandhapāṣāṇavaty upatyakā śiśiram idam indīvarāravindamakarandabinducandrakottaraṃ gotravāri ramyo 'yam anekavarṇakusumamañjarīmañjulataras taruvanābhogaḥ ity atṛptatarayā dṛśā bahu bahu paśyann alakṣitādhyārūḍhakṣoṇīdharaśikharaḥ śoṇībhūtam utprabhābhiḥ padmarāgasopānaśilābhiḥ kim api nālīkaparāgadhūsaraṃ saraḥ samadhyagamam | tatra snātaś ca kāmś=cid amṛtasvādūn bisabhaṅgān āsvādya amsalagnakalhāras tāravartinā kena api bhīmarūpeṇa brahmarākṣasena abhipatya ' ko 'si kutastyo 'si ' iti nirbhartsayatā abhyadhīye | nirbhayena ca mayā so 'bhyadhīyata - ' saumya so aham asmi dvijanmā | śatruhastād arṇavam arṇavād yavananāvam yavananāvaś citragrāvāṇam enaṃ parvatapravaraṃ gato yadṛcchayā asmin sarasi viśrāntaḥ | bhadraṃ tava ' iti | so 'brūta - ' na ced bravīṣi praśnān aśnāmi tvām ' iti | mayoktam - ' pṛcchā tāvad bhavatu ' iti | athāvayor ekayāryayāsīt samlāpaḥ - kiṃ krūraṃ strīhṛdayaṃ kiṃ gṛhiṇaḥ priyahitāya dāraguṇāḥ | kaḥ kāmaḥ saṅkalpaḥ kiṃ duṣkarasādhanaṃ prajñā || ' tatra dhūminīgominīnimbavatīnitambavatyaḥ pramāṇam | ' ity upadiṣṭo mayā so 'brūta - ' kathaya kīdṛśyas tāḥ ' iti | atrodāharam -
children.translated_text: And I, agitated by <s>Anaṅga</s> (the god of love), having gone to my own residence, was made by <s>Kośadāsa</s> to enjoy with great care a most generous provision of bathing, food, and the rest. In the evening, <s>Candrasenā</s> approached me, and having prostrated before me in private, pressing her husband's shoulder against my shoulder with tender affection, she instructed me. And <s>Kośadāsa</s>, delighted, said: 'May I be thus, for as long as I live, the recipient of your favor, O long-eyed one!' But I said with a smile: 'Friend, why wish for this? There is a certain collyrium. When her eyes are anointed with it by this woman, the prince, upon seeing her, will perceive her as a monkey-woman and, repulsed, will abandon her again.' She, smiling, said to me: 'This servant, obedient to the noble one's command, is excessively favored — in that, in this very birth, her human form will be removed and she will be made into a monkey-woman! But let that be. Our desire is already accomplished by other means as well. For today, at the ball-festival (<s>kandukotsava</s>), the princess, desiring you whose appearance betrayed the agitation of love, was excessively tormented by the Enemy of <s>Śambara</s> (<s>Kāma</s>), as if from anger. This matter, since I know the true state of affairs, will be reported by me to my own mother, by her to the princess's mother, and by the chief queen to the king. And the king, knowing the matter, will have you take his daughter's hand. And thereafter the prince will have to become your subordinate. For this is the course ordained by the gods. And when the kingdom is under your authority, <s>Bhīmadhanvan</s> will certainly not be able to transgress you and confine me. So let these three or four days be endured.' Thus addressing me and embracing her beloved, she returned. For both <s>Kośadāsa</s> and me, speculating at length in accordance with what she had said, the night somehow passed. At the end of the night, having performed my customary observances, I went to that same garden-spot, lovely with the sight of my beloved. There too, the prince approached me and, without arrogance, sat for a while entertaining me with agreeable conversation. Having taken me to a guest-chamber, he attended to me with bathing, food, bedding, and the rest befitting his own equal. And as I lay on the bed, experiencing in sleep the joy of embracing and beholding my beloved, they bound me with an iron fetter — exceedingly strong, [applied] by many powerful men who seized my stout arms. And he suddenly assailed me as I awoke: 'O fool! The speech of the doomed <s>Candrasenā</s> was overheard issuing through a lattice-opening by this hunchback woman, who was set to the task of discovering that very thing. You, it seems, are desired by the wretched <s>Kandukavatyā</s>; I, it seems, am to remain your subordinate, obedient to your word; and I, it seems, am to give <s>Candrasenā</s> to <s>Kośadāsa</s>!' Having said this, and looking at an attendant standing nearby, he declared: 'Throw this man into the sea.' And that man, as overjoyed as if he had obtained a kingdom, saying 'My lord, as you command,' did as he was ordered. But I, without any support, thrashing about with my arms this way and that, clasped to my chest some piece of wood granted by fate, and floated for so long that the day departed and the entire night [passed as well]. At dawn, some vessel came into sight. Aboard it were <s>Yavanas</s> (foreigners). They, having pulled me out, told the ship-captain named <s>Rāmeṣu</s>: 'Some unknown man has been found in the water, still bound in iron fetters.' 'This one too could water a thousand grapevines in a single moment!' [they said]. At that very instant, some pirate, surrounded by many boats, charged toward us. The <s>Yavanas</s> were terrified. Then the swift boats, like dogs surrounding a boar, closed in upon our vessel. And a battle commenced. The <s>Yavanas</s> were being defeated. Seeing them helpless and sinking, I rallied them and said: 'Remove my fetters! Here I am — I shall destroy your enemies!' They did so. And all those adversaries — with my bow <s>Śārṅga</s>, terrible in its twanging sound, showering <s>bhalla</s> (broad-headed) arrows — I cut to pieces, limb by limb. Leaping onto the boat that was lashed to our vessel, the army aboard it slain and scattered, I rushed at the ship-captain there, who did not flee, and seized him alive. And he turned out to be none other than that very <s>Bhīmadhanvan</s>. Recognizing him, I addressed him, now stricken with shame: 'Well, father, have you seen the sport of Fate?' And those sailors, having bound him exceedingly tightly with my very own chain, raised a joyous cry of exultation and worshipped me as well. But that uncontrollable ship, driven by an untimely wind, hurtled far and clung fast to some island. There, desiring sweet drinking water, firewood, roots, tubers, and fruits, we descended past a firmly embedded ring of rocks. And there was a great mountain. And I, [thinking] 'Ah, how lovely is this slope of the mountain! How charming is this foothill region with its fragrant mineral stones! How cool is this mountain stream, surpassing the <s>candrakānta</s> (moonstone) with drops of nectar from blue lotuses and day-lotuses!' — gazing with an ever more unsatisfied eye at sight after sight, having unknowingly ascended to the peak of the mountain, I came upon a lake reddened by the luster of ruby staircase-slabs, somewhat grey with the pollen of lotuses. Having bathed there and tasting certain lotus-stalk morsels sweet as ambrosia, with a <s>kalhāra</s> (white water-lily) clinging to my shoulder, I was suddenly attacked by some terrifying <s>Brahmarākṣasa</s> (a brahmin demon) dwelling on a star[-lit peak], who, seizing me, threatened: 'Who are you? Where are you from?' And I, fearless, replied to him: 'Good sir, I am a twice-born (<s>dvijanman</s>). From an enemy's hand to the ocean, from the ocean to a <s>Yavana</s> ship, from the <s>Yavana</s> ship to this excellent mountain of variegated stones — I have come by chance, and I am resting at this lake. Blessings upon you.' He said: 'If you do not answer my questions, I shall devour you.' I said: 'Let the questions be asked.' Then, between the two of us, there was a dialogue in a single verse (<s>āryā</s>): "What is cruel? A woman's heart. What are the virtues of a wife for the welfare and benefit of a householder? What is desire? A mental fancy. What accomplishes the difficult? Wisdom." 'Regarding these matters, the <s>Dhūminī</s>, <s>Gominī</s>, <s>Nimbavatī</s>, and <s>Nitambavatī</s> are the authorities.' Thus instructed by me, he said: 'Tell me — what are they like?' Here is the illustration —

praṇaya-peśalam āghaṭṭayanty upādiśat | ācaṣṭa ca hṛṣṭaḥ kośa-dāsaḥ -- ' bhūyāsam evam yāvad-āyur āyata-akṣi tvat-prasādasya pātram iti | mayā tu sa-smitam abhihitam -- ' sakhe kim etad āśāsyam | asti kiñ=cid añjanam | anayā tad-akta-netrayā rāja-sūnur upasthito vānarīm iva enāṃ drakṣyati viraktaś ca enāṃ punas tyakṣyati ' iti | tayā tu smerayā asmi kathitaḥ -- ' so 'yam āryeṇā ajñā-karo jano 'tyartham anugṛhītaḥ yad asminn eva janmani mānuṣaṃ vapur apanīya vānarīkariṣyate | tad āstām idam | anyathā api siddhaṃ naḥ samīhitam | adya khalu kanduka-utsave bhavantam avahasita-mano-bhava-ākāram abhilaṣantī roṣād iva śambara-dviṣā atimātram āyāsyate rāja-putrī | so 'yam artho vidita-bhāvayā mayā sva-mātre tayā ca tan-mātre mahiṣyā ca manuja-indrāya nivedayiṣyate | vidita-arthas tu pārthivas tvayā duhituḥ pāṇiṃ grāhayiṣyati | tataś ca tvad-anujīvinā rāja-putreṇa bhavitavyam | eṣa hi devatā-samādiṣṭo vidhiḥ | tvad-āyatte ca rājye na alam eva tvām atikramya mām avaroddhum bhīma-dhanvā | tat kṛta-yathā-ucita-niyamas tam eva priyā-darśana-subhagam udyāna-uddeśam upagato 'smi | tatra eva ca upasṛtya rāja-putro nir-abhimānam anukūlābhiḥ kathābhir mām anuvartamāno muhūrtam āsta | nītvā ca upakāryām ātma-samena snāna-bhojana-śayana-ādi-vyatikareṇa upācarat | talpa-gataṃ ca svapnena anubhūyamāna-priyā-darśana-āliṅgana-sukham āyasena nigaḍena ati-balavad-bahu-puruṣaiḥ pīvara-bhuja-daṇḍa-uparuddham abandhayan mām | pratibuddhaṃ ca sahasā samabhyadhāt -- ' ayi dur-mate śrutam ālapitaṃ hatāyāś candra-senāyā jāla-randhra-niḥsṛtaṃ tad-eka-avabodha-prayuktayā anayā kubjayā | tvaṃ kila abhilaṣito varākyā kandukavatyā tava kila anujīvinā mayā stheyam tvad-vacaḥ kila an-atikramatā mayā candra-senā kośa-dāsāya dāsyate ity uktvā pārśva-caraṃ puruṣam ekam ālokya daiva-dattam urasa ūpaśliṣya tāvad aploṣi yāvad apāsarad vāsaraḥ śarvarī ca sarvā | pratyuṣasy adṛśyata kim=api vahitram | amutrā asan yavanāḥ | te mām uddhṛtya rāma-iṣu-nāmne nāvika-nāyakāya kathitavantaḥ -- ' ko 'py ayam āyasa-nigaḍa-baddha eva jale labdhaḥ puruṣaḥ | so 'yam api siñcet sahasraṃ drākṣāṇāṃ kṣaṇena ekena iti | asminn eva kṣaṇe na-eka-naukā-parivṛtaḥ ko 'pi madgur abhyadhāvat | abibhayur yavanāḥ | tāvad ati-javā naukāḥ śvāna iva varāham asmat-potaṃ paryarutsata | prāvartata ca samprahāraḥ | parājāyiṣata yavanāḥ | tān aham a-gatīn avasīdataḥ samāśvāsya alapiṣam -- ' apanayata me nigaḍa-bandhanam | ayam aham avasādayāmi vaḥ sapatnān ' iti | amī tathā akurvan | sarvāmś ca tān pratibhaṭān bhalla-varṣiṇā bhīma-ṭaṅkṛtena śārṅgeṇa lava-lavīkṛta-aṅgān akārṣam | avaplutya hata-vidhvasta-yodham asmat-pota-samsakta-potam amutra nāvika-nāyakam an-abhisaram abhipatya jīva-grāham agrahīṣam | asau cā asīt sa eva bhīma-dhanvā | taṃ ca aham avabudhya jāta-vrīḍam abravam -- ' tāta kiṃ dṛṣṭāni kṛtānta-vilasitāni ' iti | te tu sāmyātrikā madīyena eva śṛṅkhalena tam ati-gāḍhaṃ baddhvā harṣa-kilakilā-ravam akurvan māṃ ca apy apūjayan | dur-vārā tu sā naur an-anukāla-vāta-nunnā dūram abhipatya kam api dvīpaṃ nibiḍam āśliṣṭavatī | tatra ca svādu pānīyam edhāmsi kanda-mūla-phalāni ca sañjighṛkṣavo gāḍha-pātita-śilā-valayam avātarāma | tatra cā asīn mahā-śailaḥ | so 'ham -- ' aho ramaṇīyo 'yaṃ parvata-nitamba-bhāgaḥ kāntatara īyaṃ gandha-pāṣāṇavaty upatyakā śiśiram idam indīvara-aravinda-makaranda-bindu-candraka-uttaraṃ gotra-vāri ramyo 'yam an-eka-varṇa-kusuma-mañjarī-mañjulataras taru-vana-ābhogaḥ ity a-tṛptatarayā dṛśā bahu bahu paśyann a-lakṣita-adhyārūḍha-kṣoṇī-dhara-śikharaḥ śoṇībhūtam utprabhābhiḥ padma-rāga-sopāna-śilābhiḥ kim api nālīka-parāga-dhūsaraṃ saraḥ samadhyagamam | tatra snātaś ca kāmś=cid amṛta-svādūn bisa-bhaṅgān āsvādya amsa-lagna-kalhāras tāra-vartinā kena api bhīma-rūpeṇa brahma-rākṣasena abhipatya ' ko 'si kutastyo 'si ' iti nirbhartsayatā abhyadhīye | nir-bhayena ca mayā so 'bhyadhīyata -- ' saumya so aham asmi dvi-janmā | śatru-hastād arṇavam arṇavād yavana-nāvam yavana-nāvaś citra-grāvāṇam enaṃ parvata-pravaraṃ gato yad-ṛcchayā asmin sarasi viśrāntaḥ | bhadraṃ tava ' iti | so 'brūta -- ' na ced bravīṣi praśnān aśnāmi tvām ' iti | maya ūktam -- ' pṛcchā tāvad bhavatu ' iti | athā avayor ekayā āryayā āsīt samlāpaḥ -- kiṃ krūraṃ strī-hṛdayaṃ kiṃ gṛhiṇaḥ priya-hitāya dāra-guṇāḥ | kaḥ kāmaḥ saṅkalpaḥ kiṃ duṣ-kara-sādhanaṃ prajñā || ' tatra dhūminī-gominī-nimbavatī-nitambavatyaḥ pramāṇam | ' ity upadiṣṭo mayā so 'brūta -- ' kathaya kīdṛśyas tāḥ ' iti | atra udāharam --

' asti trigarto nāma janapadaḥ | tatrāsan gṛhiṇas trayaḥ sphītasāradhanāḥ sodaryā dhanakadhānyakadhanyakākhyāḥ | teṣu jīvatsu na vavarṣa varṣāṇi dvādaśa daśaśatākṣaḥ | kṣīṇasāraṃ sasyam oṣadhyo vandhyāḥ na phalavanto vanaspatayaḥ klībā meghāḥ kṣīṇasrotasaḥ sravantyaḥ paṅkaśeṣāṇi palvalāni nirnisyandāny utsamaṇḍalāni viralībhūtaṃ kandamūlaphalam avahīnāḥ kathāḥ galitāḥ kalyāṇotsavakriyāḥ bahulībhūtāni taskarakulāni anyoanyam abhakṣayan prajāḥ paryaluṭhann itastato balākāpāṇḍurāṇi naraśiraḥkapālāni paryahiṇḍanta śuṣkāḥ kākamaṇḍalyaḥ śūnyībhūtāni nagaragrāmakharvaṭapuṭabhedanādīni | tae ete gṛhapatayaḥ sarvadhānyanicayam upayujya ajāvikaṃ gavalagaṇaṃ gavāṃ yūthaṃ dāsīdāsajanam apatyāni jyeṣṭhamadhyamabhārye ca krameṇa bhakṣayitvā ' kaniṣṭhabhāryā dhūminī śvo bhakṣaṇīyā ' iti samakalpayan | ayaṃ kaniṣṭho dhanyakaḥ priyāṃ svām attum akṣamas tayā saha tasyām eva niśy apāsarat | mārgaklāntāṃ codvahan vanaṃ jagāhe | svamāmsāsṛgapa nītakṣutpipāsāṃ tāṃ nayann antare kam api nikṛttapāṇipādakarṇanāsikam avanipṛṣṭhe viceṣṭamānaṃ puruṣam adrākṣīt | tam apy ārdrāśayaḥ skandhenodvahan kandamūlamṛgabahule gahanoddeśe yatnaracitaparṇaśālaś ciram avasat | amuṃ ca ropitavraṇam iṅgudītailādibhir āmiṣeṇa śākenātmanirviśeṣaṃ pupoṣa | puṣṭaṃ ca tam udriktadhātum ekadā mṛgānveṣaṇāya ca prayāte dhanyake sā dhūminī riramsayopātiṣṭhat | bhartsitā api tena balātkāram arīramat | nivṛttaṃ ca patim udakābhyarthinam ' uddhṛtya kūpāt piba rujati me śiraḥ śirorogaḥ ' ity udañcanaṃ sarajjuṃ puraś cikṣepa | udañcantaṃ ca taṃ kūpād apaḥ kṣaṇāt pṛṣṭhato gatvā praṇunoda | taṃ ca vikalaṃ skandhenoduhya deśād deśāntaraṃ paribhramantī pativratāpratītiṃ lebhe bahuvidhāś ca pūjāḥ | punar avantirājānugrahād atimahatyā bhūtyā nyavasat | atha pānīyārthisārthajanasamāpattidṛṣṭoddhṛtam avantiṣu bhramantam āhārārthinaṃ bhartāram upalabhya sā dhūminī ' yena me patir vikalīkṛtaḥ sa durātmā ayam ' iti tasya sādhoś citravadham ajñena rājñā samādeśayāṃ cakāra | dhanyakas tu dattapaścādbandhaḥ vadhyabhūmiṃ nīyamānaḥ saśeṣatvād āyuṣaḥ ' yo mayā vikalī kṛto 'bhimato bhikṣuḥ sa cen me pāpam ācakṣīta yukto me daṇḍaḥ ' ity adīnam adhikṛtaṃ jagāda | ' ko doṣaḥ ' ity upanīya darśite 'muṣmin sa vikalaḥ paryaśruḥ pādapatitas tasya sādhos tatsukṛtam asatyāś ca tasyās tathābhūtaṃ duścaritam āryabuddhir ācacakṣe | kupitena rājñā virūpitamukhī sā duṣkṛtakāriṇī kṛtā śvabhyaḥ pācikā | kṛtaś ca dhanyakaḥ prasādabhūmiḥ | tad bravīmi - ' strī hṛdayaṃ krūram ' iti |
children.translated_text: 'There is a country called <s>Trigarta</s>. There lived three householders, brothers, wealthy in abundant riches, named <s>Dhanaka</s>, <s>Dhānyaka</s>, and <s>Dhanyaka</s>. While they were living, the Thousand-Eyed One (<s>Indra</s>) did not send rain for twelve years. The grain lost its essence, herbs became barren, trees bore no fruit, clouds were impotent, the streams shrank in flow, the ponds were reduced to mud, the springs ceased flowing, roots, tubers, and fruits became scarce, conversation dwindled, auspicious festival rites faded away, bands of thieves multiplied, the people ate one another, human skulls white as cranes rolled about here and there, dried-up flocks of crows wandered about, and cities, villages, hamlets, and settlements were emptied. Then these householders, having consumed their entire store of grain, progressively devoured their flocks of goats and sheep, their herds of buffalo, their herds of cattle, their male and female servants, their children, and their eldest and middle wives, and resolved: "<s>Dhūminī</s>, the youngest wife, shall be eaten tomorrow." The youngest brother, <s>Dhanyaka</s>, unable to eat his beloved, fled with her that very night. Carrying her when she was exhausted from the journey, he entered the forest. Leading her — her hunger and thirst allayed by his own flesh and blood — he spotted on the way a man writhing on the ground whose hands, feet, ears, and nose had been cut off. Being tender-hearted, he carried that man too on his shoulder and, in a dense forest tract abounding in roots, tubers, and game, built a hut of leaves with great effort and dwelt there for a long time. He nursed the man, healing his wounds with <s>iṅgudī</s> oil and the like, and nourished him with meat and vegetables, no differently from himself. Once the man had been restored to health and was vigorous in constitution, one day when <s>Dhanyaka</s> had gone out to hunt game, <s>Dhūminī</s> approached the man with amorous intent. Though rebuked by him, she gratified herself by force. When her husband returned, asking for water, she threw before him the bucket with its rope, saying: "Draw it from the well and drink — my head hurts from a headache." And as he was drawing water from the well, she went behind him in an instant and pushed him in. She then carried the crippled man on her shoulder and, wandering from region to region, gained the reputation of a devoted wife and received manifold honors. Later, by the grace of the king of <s>Avanti</s>, she lived in very great prosperity. Then <s>Dhūminī</s>, encountering her husband — who had been discovered by chance by traveling merchants seeking water, pulled out of the well, and was wandering about in the <s>Avanti</s> country seeking food — told the ignorant king: "This wicked person is the one who mutilated my husband!" and had a gruesome execution ordered for that virtuous man. But <s>Dhanyaka</s>, seized and bound and being led to the execution ground, since his lifespan was not yet exhausted, fearlessly declared to the officer: "If the honored mendicant whom I mutilated were to accuse me of the crime, then my punishment would be just." "What is the harm?" they said, and when the man was brought before him, the cripple, tearful and falling at the feet of that good man, with noble-minded [candor], told the truth about the virtuous man's good deed and the faithless woman's wicked conduct. The enraged king had that evildoer's face disfigured and made her a cook for the dogs. And <s>Dhanyaka</s> was shown royal favor. Therefore I say: "The heart of a woman is cruel."'

' ebhir labdhāḥ kākiṇīr datvā śākaṃ ghṛtaṃ dadhi tailam āmalakaṃ ciñcāphalaṃ ca yathālābham ānaya ' iti | tathā anuṣṭhite ca tayā dvitrān upadamśān upapādya tadannamaṇḍam ārdravālukopahitanavaśarāvagatam atimṛdunā tālavṛntānilena śītalīkṛtya salavaṇasambhāraṃ dattāṅgāradhūpavāsaṃ ca sampādya tad apy āmalakaṃ ślakṣṇapiṣṭam utpalagandhi kṛtvā dhātrīmukhena snā nāya tam acodayat | tayā ca snānaśuddhayā dattatailāmalakaḥ krameṇa sasnau | snātaḥ siktamṛṣṭe kuṭṭime phalakam āruhya pāṇḍuharitasya tribhāgaśeṣalūnasya aṅgaṇakadalīpalāśasyopari śarāvadvayaṃ dattam ārdram abhimṛśann atiṣṭhat | sā tu tāṃ peyām eva agre samupāharat | pītvā ca apanatādhvaklamaḥ prahṛṣṭaḥ praklinnasakalagātraḥ sthito 'bhūt | tatas tasya śālyodanasya darvīdvayaṃ datvā sarpirmā trāṃ sūpam upadamśaṃ copajahāra | imaṃ ca dadhnā ca trijātakāvacūrṇitena surabhiśītalābhyāṃ ca kālaśeyakāñjikābhyāṃ śeṣam annam abhojayat | saśeṣae eva andhasy asāv atṛpyat | ayācata ca pānīyam | atha navabhṛṅgārasambhṛtam agurudhūpadhūpitam abhinavapāṭalīkusumavāsitam utphullotpalagrathitasaurabhaṃ vāri nālīdhārātmanā pātayāṃ babhūva | so 'pi mukhopahitaśarāveṇa himaśiśirakaṇakarālitāruṇāyamānākṣipakṣmā dhārāravābhinanditaśravaṇaḥ sparśasukhodbhinnaromāñcakarkaśakapolaḥ parimalapravālotpīḍaphullaghrāṇarandhro mādhuryaprakarṣāvarjitarasanendriyas tad acchaṃ pānīyam ākaṇṭhaṃ papau | śiraḥkampasaṃjñāvāritā ca punar aparakarakeṇācamanam adatta kanyā | vṛddhayā tu taducchiṣṭam apohya haritagomayopalipte kuṭṭime svam evottarīyakarpaṭaṃ vyavadhāya kṣaṇam aśeta | parituṣṭaś ca vidhivad upayamya kanyāṃ ninye | nītvaitadanapekṣaḥ kām=api gaṇikām avarodham akarot | tām apy asau priyasakhīm ivopācarat | patiṃ ca daivatam iva muktatandrā paryacarat | gṛhakāryāṇi ca ahīnam anvatiṣṭhat | parijanaṃ ca dākṣiṇyanidhir ātmādhīnam akarot | tadguṇavaśīkṛtaś ca bhartā sarvam eva kuṭumbaṃ tadāyattam eva kṛtvā tadekādhīnajīvitaśarīras trivargaṃ nirviveśa | tad bravīmi -' gṛhiṇaḥ priyahitāya dāraguṇāḥ ' iti |
children.translated_text: Asked again, he related the tale of <s>Gominī</s>: 'There is in the <s>Draviḍa</s> country a city named <s>Kāñcī</s>. In it there was a merchant's son named <s>Śaktikumāra</s>, possessed of wealth of many crores. He, being about eighteen years of age, fell to brooding: "There is no happiness, surely, for those who are wifeless, nor for those whose wives are uncongenial. How then might I obtain a wife endowed with virtues?" Then, not regarding as fortunate a wife brought to him on the strength of others' judgment, he became an astrologer and wandered the land with a prastha-measure of rice tied up in the corner of his garment. 'This man knows the marks [of good fortune],' [thinking thus,] those who had daughters displayed their daughters to him. And on seeing some maiden marked with auspicious signs and of good caste, he would say, so they tell: 'Good lady, are you able with this prastha of rice to prepare and serve us food endowed with good qualities?' Shaken off with laughter, he entered house after house and roamed about. But one day, among the <s>Śibis</s>, in a port-town on the bank of the <s>Kāverī</s>, he beheld a certain maiden being shown to him by her nurse—a girl scantily adorned, [of a family] whose great prosperity had run out together with her parents, whose mansion's wealth had crumbled away. And with his eyes fixed upon her, he reasoned: 'Indeed, all the limbs of this maiden are neither too stout nor too lean, neither too short nor too long, not unshapely, and well-kept. Her two hands are red-palmed, marked with auspicious lines of barley, fish, lotus, water-jar, and the like; her two feet have even ankle-joints, are fleshy and not veiny; her two shins are tapering in due succession; her knees, swallowed up as it were by the plump thighs, are hard to discern; her hip-region is well-divided at one stroke, square, lovely with the curve of the dimples, and shaped like the circle of a wheel; her belly is very slender, slightly hollowed, with a deep navel-circle, and adorned with the three folds; her breasts, rising upon the expanse of her bosom, with up-tilted nipples, are charming with their broad swell; her two hands, their palms marked with lines that betoken abundance of wealth, grain, and sons, have smooth, tapering, soft nail-gems; her two arm-creepers, with copper-red fingers straight and tapering in due succession, with shoulders evenly sloped, are tender and have their joint-knuckles sunk in; her neck is slender, curved and round like a conch; her lower lip is red, set off by the rounded middle [of her mouth]; her chin is not shrunken and lovely; her cheek-circle is full and firm; her brow-creepers are unjoined, gently arched, dark and glossy; her nose resembles a sesame-flower not over-grown; her eyes, brilliant in their three parts of dark, white, and red, are sweet, steady, slow-moving, and long; her forehead is lovely as the crescent moon; her pair of ears, with the line of her locks doubly curled like slabs of sapphire, are graceful and long like the faded stalks of lotus-fibre—such is her lotus-face; her mass of hair is not too curly, abundant, not tawny even at the tips, long, each strand by nature smooth, dark, and even, and fragrant. This form does not belie good character. And my heart clings to her alone. So let me marry her after testing her. For surely upon the rash actor fall many an endless train of regrets.' And so, with a tender gaze, he said: 'Good lady, is there skill [enough] in you to prepare and serve us a complete meal with this prastha of rice?' Thereupon she was glanced at meaningfully by the old serving-woman. Taking from his hand the mere prastha of grain, she seated him in some part of the courtyard, well-sprinkled and swept, and gave him water to wash his feet. That maiden, having pounded those fragrant rice-grains a little and dried them in the sun, turning them again and again, then upon firm, level ground rubbing them ever so gently with the back of a reed, separated the rice-grains from the unbroken husks. And she said to the nurse: 'Mother, these husks are sought after by goldsmiths as fit for the cleaning and polishing of ornaments. Giving these to them and with the kākiṇī-coins thus obtained, fetch firm pieces of wood, neither too damp nor too dry, a cooking-pot that boils a measured amount, and two earthen bowls.' When that was done by her, she put those rice-grains into a mortar of <s>kakubha</s>-wood, with a hollow neither too sunken nor too flat but broad, with a pestle of <s>khadira</s>-wood—iron-rimmed at the mouth, even of body, of perceptibly slender middle, long, heavy—and, her arm wearied by the graceful raising and lowering [of the pestle], lifting them up again and again with her fingers and pounding, winnowing away the chaff-dust with a winnowing-basket, washing the cleaned rice-grains repeatedly with water, she cast them into water boiled fivefold, having first paid honor to the hearth. When the rice-grains, their bodies loosening and swelling, had passed beyond the budding stage, drawing back the fire, she strained off the rice-water with the pot whose mouth-lid was set in place. And stirring with the ladle and turning [the rice] a little, when the grains were evenly cooked, she set that pot down mouth-downward. The fuel, being of solid pith, she sprinkled with water and, having quenched its fire and reduced it to black charcoal, she sent it to those who wanted it [saying]: 'Giving the kākiṇīs obtained for these, fetch vegetables, ghee, curds, oil, myrobalan, and tamarind-fruit, as may be had.' And when this too was done by her, having prepared two or three relishes, and having cooled that rice-water—set in a fresh earthen bowl placed upon moist sand—with a very soft breeze from a palm-leaf fan, having seasoned it with salt and perfumed it with the incense of burning charcoal, and having also made that myrobalan into a fine paste fragrant as a blue lotus, she urged him to his bath through the nurse. And he, purified by the bath, anointed with oil and myrobalan, in due course bathed thoroughly. Bathed, having climbed upon a plank on the sprinkled and swept floor, he sat touching two moist earthen bowls set upon the courtyard plantain-leaf, pale-green, cut off with a third part remaining. And she first brought him the gruel. And having drunk it, his road-weariness removed, delighted, his whole body bedewed [with refreshment], he remained. Then, giving him two ladlefuls of that fine rice, she served a measure of ghee, soup, and a relish. And this rice she had him eat with curds powdered with the three spices, and with butter-milk and fragrant, cool sour-gruel for what remained. With food yet remaining, he was satisfied. And he asked for water. Then she made fall, in the form of a thread, water gathered in a fresh pitcher, perfumed with the incense of aloe-wood, scented with fresh trumpet-flowers, with a fragrance entwined of full-blown lotuses. And he too, with the bowl set to his mouth, his eyelashes reddened and made rough by the cold, cool drops [turning them] coppery, his ears gladdened by the sound of the stream, his cheeks bristling-rough with horripilation born of the pleasant touch, his nostrils opening at the gush of the fragrant essence, his organ of taste won over by the excellence of sweetness, drank that clear water up to the throat. And, stayed by the sign of a shake of his head, the maiden gave him water for rinsing the mouth with another water-jar. And the old woman, having removed his leavings, upon the floor smeared with green cow-dung, spreading her own cloth upper-garment, lay down for a moment. And, well-pleased, having married the maiden in due form, he led her away. Having led her away, indifferent to all else, he took some courtesan into his household. Her too he treated as though a dear friend. And [his wife], free from sloth, served her husband as though a deity. And the household duties she carried out without fail. And the household folk, being a treasury of courtesy, she made her own. And the husband, won over by her virtues, having made the whole household entirely dependent upon her, his life and body wholly subject to her alone, enjoyed the three aims [of life]. Therefore I say: "For the householder, the virtues of a wife are for his welfare and delight."'
